MY CAR HAD ONLY 600 MILES AND IS BRAND NEW. AFTER SITTING ON THE DRIVE OVERNIGHT THE CAR WOULDN'T START. THERE WAS A LOT OF CLICKING NOISES, BUT THE ENGINE WOULDN'T TURN. THAT WAS THREE WEEKS AGO. I BROUGHT IT TO THE DEALERSHIP AND THEY SAID THAT THERE WERE ERROR CODES ON THE BATTERY, AND THAT THEY RECHARGED IT. TODAY, THE CAR CLICKS AND WON'T TURN OVER AGAIN. THE CAR NOW HAS 1000 MILES. THE DEALERSHIP TOLD ME THAT CARS DRIVING BY THEIR LOT AT NIGHT WILL CAUSE RANDOM PARKED NEW VEHICLES WITH NO KEY IN IT TO FLASH LIGHTS, AND USE OTHER ELECTRICAL COMPONENTS RANDOMLY AND IT KILLS THE BATTERIES. I THINK THIS IS A MAJOR CONCERN. I PARK THE CAR REGULARLY IN PUBLIC LOTS AT THE AIRPORT. I CAN'T HAVE MY CAR BATTERY DEAD ALL THE TIME SIMPLY BECAUSE IT DECIDES TO TURN ON AS OTHER CARS DRIVE BY.

Complete Technical Description

 

 

 

Title: Zendood - The Self-Sustaining Autonomous Vehicle (SSAV) with Integrated Multi-Source Energy Harvesting Architecture

 

 

 

1. Technical Field

 

The present invention relates generally to the field of autonomous electric vehicles and renewable energy systems, specifically to a novel class of vehicle designed to achieve complete operational energy independence through integrated multi-source energy harvesting technologies. The invention provides an autonomous vehicle capable of generating sufficient power for its propulsion, onboard systems, and autonomous driving functions without requiring connection to external charging infrastructure or fuel supplies.

 

 

 

2. Background of the Invention

 

2.1 The Fundamental Limitation of Current Electric and Autonomous Vehicles

 

Despite rapid advancements in electric vehicle technology and autonomous driving systems, all current vehicles share a critical vulnerability: complete dependence on external energy infrastructure. This dependency manifests in several fundamental limitations:

 

Range Anxiety: Even the most advanced electric vehicles with 400+ mile ranges remain tethered to charging networks. Drivers must constantly monitor battery levels and plan routes around available charging stations, limiting spontaneity and creating stress.

 

Infrastructure Dependency: The global transition to electric mobility requires trillions of dollars in charging infrastructure investment. Rural areas, developing nations, and remote regions remain underserved, creating mobility inequity.

 

Operational Limitations for Autonomous Fleets: Autonomous vehicles intended for continuous operation (ride-sharing fleets, delivery services, emergency response) must return to charging stations periodically, reducing their effective utilization and economic viability.

 

Environmental Blind Spots: While electric vehicles produce zero tailpipe emissions, their overall carbon footprint remains tied to the grid's energy mix. In regions powered by coal or natural gas, "clean" vehicles still carry a significant environmental burden.

 

Disaster Vulnerability: During natural disasters or grid failures, electric vehicles become immobile precisely when transportation is most critical for evacuation and emerge

evidence.title: The Effect of Frequency Droop Damping on System Parameters and Battery Sizing During Load Change Condition
evidence.abstract: Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been widely studied for their advantages on the current power systems. This increase in the penetration of renewable energy has raised some concerns about the stability of the existing grid. Historically, power systems are dominated by synchronous generators that can easily react to system instability due to high inertia and damping characteristics. However, with IBR, the control of the inverter plays a crucial role in contributing to the system stability and enhancing the functionality of the inverters. One of these novel control methods is droop control. Droop characteristics are used to control voltage, frequency, and active and reactive power. This paper presents the impact of frequency droop damping on system frequency, real power, and the rate of change of frequency with distributed energy resources. Also, battery sizing is suggested based on the results. The results also show the need for optimal selection for the frequency droop damping to fulfill the appropriate battery size in terms of cost and performance. The simulations are carried out in an electromagnetic transient program (EMTP)

evidence.title: Oxygen redox in battery cathodes: A brief overview
evidence.abstract: The participation of oxygen or other anionic species in redox activities in cathode materials for lithium and sodium-ion battery systems is known to play a role in governing the useful capacity of these batteries. Directly probing anionic redox mechanisms is not possible, rather the computational analysis by density functional theory poses the main approach towards gleaning insights into anionic redox activity and harnessing these effects to maximize capacity in future electrode materials. Here we showcase material systems exhibiting this mechanism of ion insertion and removal, and present the key computational considerations in studying anionic redox activities in battery materials. Aided by new computationally derived understandings of the role of anionic redox in emerging battery materials, increasingly greater levels of useable capacities can be extracted through informed materials design.

evidence.title: Energy Harvesting Communications Using Dual Alternating Batteries
evidence.abstract: Practical energy harvesting (EH) based communication systems typically use a battery to temporarily store the harvested energy prior to its use for communication. The batteries can be damaged when they are repeatedly charged (discharged) after being partially discharged (charged), overcharged or deeply discharged. This motivates the cycle constraint which says that a battery must be charged (discharged) only after it is sufficiently discharged (charged). We also assume Bernoulli energy arrivals, and a half-duplex constraint due to which the batteries are not charged and discharged simultaneously. In this context, we study EH communication systems with: (a) a single-battery with capacity 2B units and (b) dual-batteries, each having capacity of B units. The aim is to obtain the best possible long-term average throughputs and throughput regions in point-to-point (P2P) channels and multiple access channels (MAC), respectively. For the P2P channel, we obtain an analytical optimal solution in the single-battery case, and propose optimal and sub-optimal power allocation policies for the dual-battery case. We extend these policies to obtain achievable throughput regions in MACs by jointly allocating rates and powers. From numerical simulations, we find that the optimal throughput in the dual-battery case is significantly higher than that in the single-battery case, although the total storage capacity in both cases is 2B units. Further, in the proposed policies, the largest throughput region in the single-battery case is contained within that of the dual-battery case.

mechanism_map.mechanism: Integrated multi-source energy harvesting architecture to generate power for onboard systems independent of external infrastructure.
mechanism_map.intervention: Install a dedicated low-power energy harvester (e.g., vibration or ambient RF) on the 12V battery bus to continuously offset parasitic drain from spurious RF activations, ensuring net-positive charge balance during parking without disabling the receiver.
mechanism_map.expected_effect: Elimination of battery depletion caused by unintended electrical activation while maintaining full functionality of keyless-entry and security systems.
mechanism_map.falsification_test: Park the vehicle in a controlled RF-noise environment simulating spurious triggers for 72 hours; measure 12V battery state-of-charge with the harvester active versus a control unit without the harvester.

Complete Technical Description

 

 

 

Title: Zendood - The Self-Sustaining Autonomous Vehicle (SSAV) with Integrated Multi-Source Energy Harvesting Architecture

 

 

 

1. Technical Field

 

The present invention relates generally to the field of autonomous electric vehicles and renewable energy systems, specifically to a novel class of vehicle designed to achieve complete operational energy independence through integrated multi-source energy harvesting technologies. The invention provides an autonomous vehicle capable of generating sufficient power for its propulsion, onboard systems, and autonomous driving functions without requiring connection to external charging infrastructure or fuel supplies.

 

 

 

2. Background of the Invention

 

2.1 The Fundamental Limitation of Current Electric and Autonomous Vehicles

 

Despite rapid advancements in electric vehicle technology and autonomous driving systems, all current vehicles share a critical vulnerability: complete dependence on external energy infrastructure. This dependency manifests in several fundamental limitations:

 

Range Anxiety: Even the most advanced electric vehicles with 400+ mile ranges remain tethered to charging networks. Drivers must constantly monitor battery levels and plan routes around available charging stations, limiting spontaneity and creating stress.

 

Infrastructure Dependency: The global transition to electric mobility requires trillions of dollars in charging infrastructure investment. Rural areas, developing nations, and remote regions remain underserved, creating mobility inequity.

 

Operational Limitations for Autonomous Fleets: Autonomous vehicles intended for continuous operation (ride-sharing fleets, delivery services, emergency response) must return to charging stations periodically, reducing their effective utilization and economic viability.

 

Environmental Blind Spots: While electric vehicles produce zero tailpipe emissions, their overall carbon footprint remains tied to the grid's energy mix. In regions powered by coal or natural gas, "clean" vehicles still carry a significant environmental burden.

 

Disaster Vulnerability: During natural disasters or grid failures, electric vehicles become immobile precisely when transportation is most critical for evacuation and emerge

custody_records.raw_content: Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been widely studied for their advantages on the current power systems. This increase in the penetration of renewable energy has raised some concerns about the stability of the existing grid. Historically, power systems are dominated by synchronous generators that can easily react to system instability due to high inertia and damping characteristics. However, with IBR, the control of the inverter plays a crucial role in contributing to the system stability and enhancing the functionality of the inverters. One of these novel control methods is droop control. Droop characteristics are used to control voltage, frequency, and active and reactive power. This paper presents the impact of frequency droop damping on system frequency, real power, and the rate of change of frequency with distributed energy resources. Also, battery sizing is suggested based on the results. The results also show the need for optimal selection for the frequency droop damping to fulfill the appropriate battery size in terms of cost and performance. The simulations are carried out in an electromagnetic transient program (EMTP)

custody_records.raw_content: The participation of oxygen or other anionic species in redox activities in cathode materials for lithium and sodium-ion battery systems is known to play a role in governing the useful capacity of these batteries. Directly probing anionic redox mechanisms is not possible, rather the computational analysis by density functional theory poses the main approach towards gleaning insights into anionic redox activity and harnessing these effects to maximize capacity in future electrode materials. Here we showcase material systems exhibiting this mechanism of ion insertion and removal, and present the key computational considerations in studying anionic redox activities in battery materials. Aided by new computationally derived understandings of the role of anionic redox in emerging battery materials, increasingly greater levels of useable capacities can be extracted through informed materials design.

custody_records.raw_content: Practical energy harvesting (EH) based communication systems typically use a battery to temporarily store the harvested energy prior to its use for communication. The batteries can be damaged when they are repeatedly charged (discharged) after being partially discharged (charged), overcharged or deeply discharged. This motivates the cycle constraint which says that a battery must be charged (discharged) only after it is sufficiently discharged (charged). We also assume Bernoulli energy arrivals, and a half-duplex constraint due to which the batteries are not charged and discharged simultaneously. In this context, we study EH communication systems with: (a) a single-battery with capacity 2B units and (b) dual-batteries, each having capacity of B units. The aim is to obtain the best possible long-term average throughputs and throughput regions in point-to-point (P2P) channels and multiple access channels (MAC), respectively. For the P2P channel, we obtain an analytical optimal solution in the single-battery case, and propose optimal and sub-optimal power allocation policies for the dual-battery case. We extend these policies to obtain achievable throughput regions in MACs by jointly allocating rates and powers. From numerical simulations, we find that the optimal throughput in the dual-battery case is significantly higher than that in the single-battery case, although the total storage capacity in both cases is 2B units. Further, in the proposed policies, the largest throughput region in the single-battery case is contained within that of the dual-battery case.
